text: Signal is much stronger than the noise. We are happy, we get a high SNR. If the signal instead is very weak, and its power is close to that of noise, then the SNR is low, and we are not happy because it will be very difficult for the receiver to distinguish the signal, the useful signal, from the noise. So likely in that case, when the SNR is low, the receiver will make lots of mistakes. It has problems in understanding which bits, which symbols have been transmitted, because the signal is too similar to the noise. Now another slightly different performance metric that is used to measure the quality of the signal that we that we receive is the SINR, that means signal to interference plus noise ratio. In this case, we still consider a ratio, but at the numerator we have the useful signal that we received, the power of the useful signal that is received, and the denominator instead of having only the power of the noise, we add also the power of the interfering signals coming from other transmitters. Because unfortunately in real world, we do not have only transmitter and receiver, but we may have many.
